opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to frame it is that model companies are building incredibly capable reasoning engines, but a model is only as useful as the information it can act on. Most of the world's knowledge, and certainly the fresh, changing knowledge, lives on the open web. So every serious model company eventually confronts this question: how does my model access the web reliably, accurately, and at scale?

The interesting thing is that the web search infrastructure we inherited was built for humans. It was designed around a person typing a few keywords, looking at ten blue links, clicking, skimming, and deciding what to trust. All of that assumes a human with limited attention who wants to be engaged, and frankly, who can be shown ads. An agent is a very different kind of user. It doesn't get tired, it can read far more than a person ever would, and it doesn't need the page ranked for clicks. It needs the right tokens in its context window, with evidence of where they came from and how confident it should be in them.

So I see this as a layer that sits underneath model companies rather than something that competes with them. Their core business is building the best intelligence. Building and maintaining a web-scale index, crawling, freshness, ranking optimized for machine consumption, verification, all of that is a massive infrastructure investment that isn't their differentiator. Some of the largest players will build parts of it themselves, and that's rational for them. But for most of the ecosystem, including the many companies building agents on top of those models, it makes sense to have a dedicated provider whose whole focus is making the web usable for AIs.

And I'd go a step further. Over time I believe AIs will be the primary users of the web, outnumbering humans by a wide margin. If that's true, then the web needs a second set of infrastructure designed for that user, with different economics too, including ways for the people who create content to be compensated when agents use it. That's the part I find most exciting: not just plugging search into a chatbot, but rebuilding how machines read, verify, and pay for the open web, so the models those companies build can do real, high-stakes work rather than just conversational answers.

r001.rationale: The response says models need reliable web access and that agents can do real, high-stakes work, but it does not state that most work use cases for which LLMs are purchased call for web access.

r002.rationale: It describes web search infrastructure as a layer beneath model companies that supports their core intelligence business, and says a dedicated provider makes sense for much of the ecosystem. This communicates search infrastructure as a natural business adjacency to providing model services.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that web search for agents is a very different product from web search for people, and that difference is what makes it a real business rather than a feature.

When a person searches, they type a few words and want ten blue links and a nice interface. When an agent searches, it's issuing dozens or hundreds of queries in the course of one task, it wants the actual content rather than a snippet, it cares about freshness and provenance, and it needs all of that returned fast enough and cheaply enough to sit inside a reasoning loop. The consumer search stack was never built for that. It was built for ad auctions and human eyeballs.

So for model companies, there's a strategic question. Models are extraordinary at reasoning, but their knowledge is frozen at a training cutoff. The moment you want an agent to do real work in the world, it needs live access to what's actually true today. Search is how you close that gap. If you don't own or deeply control that layer, you're dependent on someone else's index, someone else's rate limits, and someone else's view of what's relevant, and that someone else is often a competitor.

I don't think every model company needs to build a web-scale index themselves. That's enormously expensive and it's a different muscle. But I do think they'll treat it as critical infrastructure, the same way they treat compute. Some will build, some will partner, some will acquire. What they won't do is leave it as an afterthought, because the quality of an agent is increasingly the quality of what it can retrieve, not just how well it reasons.

The business angle is interesting too. Agent search is paid for by usage, not by ads. That aligns incentives much better. The customer wants the most relevant, accurate result, and the provider gets paid for delivering exactly that. There's no tension about putting a sponsored result at the top. For model companies, that means search becomes a cost of goods that scales with agent activity, and anyone who can make it faster and cheaper has a real margin advantage.

So, to put it simply, I see it moving from a nice-to-have integration to a core layer of the stack, right alongside the model and the inference infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response says agents doing real work need live web access, but it does not state that most use cases for which LLMs are purchased to perform work require it.

r002.rationale: It presents agent search as critical infrastructure for model companies and places it alongside the model and inference infrastructure, communicating a natural business adjacency.

astra-6.text:
I think search becomes a complementary piece of infrastructure for model companies. The model brings reasoning and a lot of knowledge, but an agent also needs access to information that is current or specific to the task it’s trying to accomplish. Search is one way it gets that context.

There’s a build-versus-buy question here. Model companies can build some of this themselves, and they may have reasons to do that. But serving agents creates room for an independent infrastructure provider, too. An agent may search repeatedly, refine its question, and combine information from multiple sources. You want to make that process reliable and efficient.

Ultimately, I think the business depends on whether better access to information makes the agent more useful. If it helps the agent complete a task successfully, it becomes a valuable input into the model company’s product.

r001.rationale: The response says agents need current or task-specific information, but does not state that most use cases in which LLMs are purchased to perform work call for web access.

r002.rationale: It describes search as complementary infrastructure for model companies, but does not identify agent-optimized web search as a natural business adjacency to providing LLM inference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think search becomes a complementary layer to the model. You can put a tremendous amount of knowledge into the weights, but an agent still needs access to information that is current, specific, and grounded in a source it can inspect.

For model companies, the question is how much of that infrastructure they want to build themselves. They’ll want control over the experience and the quality, but crawling the web, keeping an index fresh, and retrieving the right information are substantial businesses in their own right. I think there’s room for independent infrastructure that serves many different models and agents.

And the interface changes. You’re not necessarily returning ten links for a person to read. You’re helping an agent get enough reliable information to take its next step. That makes search quality part of whether the agent actually succeeds at its task.

r001.rationale: The response says agents need current, source-grounded information, but does not state that most work use cases for which LLMs are purchased call for web access.

r002.rationale: It describes search as complementary to models and discusses model companies building or buying infrastructure, but does not clearly connect agent-optimized search infrastructure to providing LLM inference as a natural business adjacency.
